reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A syndrome of recurrent episodes of mast cell mediator release affecting two or more organ systems, typically skin, gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular and respiratory systems
Common features include flushing, urticaria, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, hypotension and, in severe cases, anaphylaxis
Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture, objective evidence of mediator release, and a response to mast-cell-directed treatment
A transient rise in serum tryptase measured during and after an event, compared with a stable baseline, provides objective support
The syndrome is classified as primary (clonal, with a KIT D816V mutation or the surface marker CD25), secondary (an identifiable allergic or other trigger), or idiopathic
It overlaps with, but must be distinguished from, systemic mastocytosis, which shows a clonal expansion of mast cells
Management combines trigger avoidance with agents that block or stabilise mast cell mediators, such as antihistamines and mast cell stabilisers, and adrenaline for anaphylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: Mast cell activation syndrome arises from inappropriate or excessive release of mast cell mediators, including histamine, tryptase, prostaglandins and leukotrienes, producing multisystem symptoms. In primary (clonal) disease an acquired activating KIT D816V mutation, often with aberrant CD25 expression, lowers the threshold for mast cell degranulation. In secondary forms an identifiable trigger such as IgE-mediated allergy drives activation, while idiopathic cases have no demonstrable clone or trigger. The released mediators cause vasodilatation, increased vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction and secretory changes that explain the flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm and gastrointestinal symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Vasoactive intestinal peptide or other neuroendocrine tumour
additionalInvestigations: Serial serum tryptase with an event-related rise above baseline
Urinary mediators such as N-methylhistamine and prostaglandin metabolites
KIT D816V mutation testing in blood or marrow
Bone marrow examination with mast cell immunophenotyping when clonal disease is suspected
Exclusion tests for carcinoid and phaeochromocytoma where indicated
redFlags: Recurrent anaphylaxis or unexplained hypotensive collapse
A persistently and markedly elevated baseline tryptase suggesting clonal mast cell disease
Features of systemic mastocytosis such as organomegaly or cytopenias
Failure to respond to standard mast-cell-directed therapy
reference.prognosis: Most patients achieve good symptom control with trigger avoidance and mediator-directed therapy and have a normal life expectancy; prognosis is less favourable when there is an underlying advanced clonal mast cell disorder.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the syndrome without objective evidence of mediator release
Failing to check a baseline tryptase, so an event-related rise cannot be interpreted
Missing an underlying clonal mast cell disorder or systemic mastocytosis
Overlooking mimics such as carcinoid or phaeochromocytoma
